2.30 · Hierarchical Bayes: who sets the weights?¶

Before this: 2.08 (Bayesian linear inversion), 2.09 (smoothing priors), 2.13 (C_d and C_p), 2.18 (NUTS), 2.29 (ABIC and the marginal likelihood)
You will be able to: write a slip inversion as a hierarchy with data and smoothing weights; say when ABIC's single best setting and the fully Bayesian answer agree and when the plug-in is overconfident; see why positivity breaks the ABIC formula; read an estimated data weight as a misfit level; test how much a hyperprior matters
Optional sections: 3 (positivity and orthant probabilities)

Every slip inversion has two knobs that the physics does not set: how much to trust the data (the data weight) and how strongly to smooth the slip (the smoothing weight). Setting them by hand until the result "looks reasonable" is subjective. Two data-driven alternatives dominate the geodetic literature: ABIC (Akaike 1980; Yabuki & Matsu'ura 1992), which picks the single best setting, and the fully Bayesian (hierarchical) approach of Fukuda & Johnson (2008, 2010), which keeps every setting weighted by its probability. This notebook compares them on small problems where the exact answer is known, reproduces the two criticisms Fukuda & Johnson made of ABIC, and then shows what the estimated weights actually measure.

Words this notebook defines: hyperparameter, hyperprior, hierarchical model, marginal likelihood, ABIC, empirical Bayes, hierarchical (fully) Bayes, plug-in posterior, law of total variance, positivity, orthant probability, data weight σ_k, mixed linear–nonlinear inversion, improper prior, objective (in the sense used in this literature).

Quotes from the papers are verbatim, with journal page numbers.

Problems in this notebook

problem unknowns data forward model linear?
antiplane fault in depth (sections 1, 2, 6) 24 patches + σ², α² 5 to 120 stations on one side, σ = 2 mm (0.05 mm in one test) screw-dislocation Green's functions, $\mathbf d = \mathbf G\mathbf s$ linear in slip
along-strike creep profile (sections 2, 6) 120 patches + σ², α² 6 to 120 stations each station averages the nearby slip (Gaussian kernel) linear in slip

The fault toys use stations on one side of the fault only. With stations in mirror pairs ($\pm x$) an antiplane fault gives $u(-x) = -u(x)$, so each pair measures the same slip combination twice (notebook 2.33).

C_ABIC, C_FULL, C_CONV, C_TRUE = S.BLUE, S.VIOLET, S.ORANGE, S.INK      # ABIC / fully Bayesian / conventional / truth

def second_difference(M):
    """Second difference with zero-slip rows at both ends: full rank, as Fukuda & Johnson require for D^T D."""
    Dm = np.zeros((M, M))
    for i in range(M):
        Dm[i, i] = -2.0
        if i > 0:
            Dm[i, i - 1] = 1.0
        if i < M - 1:
            Dm[i, i + 1] = 1.0
    return Dm


def screw_G(xs, z_edges):
    """Surface displacement (mm) per metre of slip on each depth patch of a vertical strike-slip fault."""
    return 1000.0 * np.array([[(np.arctan(z_edges[j + 1] / x) - np.arctan(z_edges[j] / x)) / np.pi
                               for j in range(len(z_edges) - 1)] for x in xs])

1. The hierarchy: knobs above the slip¶

In plain words. A slip inversion has three layers. At the bottom are the data. Above them is the slip, which predicts the data through the Green's functions. Above the slip sit the knobs: σ² says how far the data may stray from the prediction, and α² says how rough the slip may be. In a hierarchical model the knobs are unknowns too. They get their own priors (hyperpriors), and the data are allowed to tell us about them.

Precisely (Fukuda & Johnson 2008, eqs 7 and 9, in the notation of these notebooks: slip $\mathbf s$, difference operator $\mathbf D$, which they call $\mathbf L$):

$$\mathbf d \mid \mathbf s, \sigma^2 \sim N(\mathbf G\mathbf s,\; \sigma^2\boldsymbol\Sigma_d), \qquad \mathbf D\mathbf s \mid \alpha^2 \sim N(\mathbf 0,\; \alpha^2\mathbf I), \qquad (\sigma^2, \alpha^2) \sim p(\sigma^2, \alpha^2).$$

Here $\boldsymbol\Sigma_d$ is the shape of the data covariance (reminder: $\mathbf C_d$, 2.07 and 2.13) and σ² scales it. The smoothing prior is $p(\mathbf s\mid\alpha^2) = (2\pi\alpha^2)^{-N_m/2}\,|\mathbf D^\top\mathbf D|^{1/2}\exp(-\lVert\mathbf D\mathbf s\rVert^2/2\alpha^2)$, where the factor in front is its normalising constant (it makes the density integrate to one; 2.29) and $|\cdot|$ is the determinant (2.06): a large α² allows rough slip, a small α² forces smooth slip. The MAP (most probable slip, 2.08) for fixed knobs minimises $\lVert\mathbf d - \mathbf G\mathbf s\rVert^2/\sigma^2 + \lVert\mathbf D\mathbf s\rVert^2/\alpha^2$, so with σ known the smoothing weight λ of notebook 2.29 is $1/\alpha^2$.

"Objective" in this literature means that no number was picked by hand after looking at the result. Fukuda & Johnson's opening sentence: "In inversion of geodetic data for spatial distribution of fault slip under smoothing and positivity constraints, subjective or incorrect techniques are often employed to select a smoothing parameter that determines the relative weight placed on fitting the data versus smoothing the slip distribution" (2008, p. 1128). It does not mean free of assumptions: the form of the smoothing operator, the noise model and the hyperpriors are still chosen by the analyst, and sections 5 and 6 show they matter.

saved figures/2-30_hierarchy.png

How to read it. Left: the model as three layers, each conditioned on the one above. Middle: the best-fitting slip (MAP) for three values of α², all computed from the same 40 data points with σ = 2 mm. With a small α² every bit of curvature is expensive, so the slip comes out smooth and too small; with a large α² the slip is free to bend and follows the noise. Right: the data minus the prediction of the true slip, for three noise levels; the displacements themselves are much larger than these deviations. Estimating the hyperparameters means asking which values of these two knobs make the observed data most plausible.

Note that α² alone does not change the shape of slip drawn from the prior: a draw is $\sqrt{\alpha^2}$ times a fixed random curve, so α² sets its size and with it the size of its curvature. The smoothing appears when the prior is balanced against the data, through the ratio α²/σ².

Common misreadings.

  • "Estimated weights remove all subjectivity." They remove the hand-picked numbers; the forms (smoothing operator, noise model, hyperprior) remain choices.
  • "α² is a regularisation trick, not a probability." In the hierarchical model it is the variance of $\mathbf D\mathbf s$, a statement about how rough slip is believed to be, and it can be estimated like any other unknown.

2. ABIC (empirical Bayes) or fully Bayesian (hierarchical Bayes)¶

In plain words. Both approaches start from the same quantity: for every setting of the knobs, how probable were the observed data, averaging over all slip models allowed by that setting? (That is the marginal likelihood; reminder: 2.12 and 2.29.) ABIC takes the single best setting and then treats it as exactly right: this "estimate the knobs as single numbers, then plug them in as if known" strategy is called empirical Bayes, and the resulting slip posterior is the plug-in posterior. The fully Bayesian approach keeps every setting, weighted by how probable it made the data, and averages the slip posteriors over them. When one setting clearly dominates, the two answers agree. When many settings are about equally good, ABIC's answer is too confident.

Precisely. The marginal likelihood (evidence) of the hyperparameters integrates the slip out: $p(\mathbf d\mid\sigma^2,\alpha^2) = \int p(\mathbf d\mid\mathbf s,\sigma^2)\,p(\mathbf s\mid\alpha^2)\,d\mathbf s$, closed form for this linear-Gaussian model. $\mathrm{ABIC} = -2\ln p(\mathbf d\mid\hat\sigma^2,\hat\alpha^2) + 2N_h$ at its minimum (Akaike 1980), and the ABIC solution is the plug-in posterior $p(\mathbf s\mid\mathbf d,\hat\sigma^2,\hat\alpha^2)$. The fully Bayesian solution is

$$p(\mathbf s\mid\mathbf d) = \iint p(\mathbf s\mid\mathbf d,\sigma^2,\alpha^2)\;p(\sigma^2,\alpha^2\mid\mathbf d)\;d\sigma^2\,d\alpha^2, \qquad p(\sigma^2,\alpha^2\mid\mathbf d)\propto p(\mathbf d\mid\sigma^2,\alpha^2)\,p(\sigma^2,\alpha^2).$$

Fukuda & Johnson (2010) state when the two agree, "If p(m, σ, α|d) has a dominant peak at its maximum" and the conditional slip posterior changes slowly near that peak (p. 1449), and when they do not: "if p(m, σ, α|d) is a broad distribution with possibly multiple peaks, p(s|d, m̃, σ̃, α̃) may be significantly different from p(s|d)" (p. 1450). In their notation m are nonlinear parameters such as fault geometry (none here) and the tilde marks the ABIC values. Their summary: "the ABIC-based method and our method can be regarded as an empirical Bayes method and a hierarchical Bayes method, respectively" (p. 1450).

Computing tool: diagonalise $\mathbf G^\top\mathbf G$ and $\mathbf D^\top\mathbf D$ together (generalised eigenvectors $\mathbf V$ with $\mathbf V^\top\mathbf D^\top\mathbf D\mathbf V = \mathbf I$, $\mathbf V^\top\mathbf G^\top\mathbf G\mathbf V = \mathrm{diag}(\mu_i)$). In words: a set of slip patterns that the prior penalises equally and that the data see independently, pattern $i$ with strength $\mu_i$ (an extension of the eigen-decomposition of 2.06). In these patterns every matrix is diagonal, so the formulas reduce to one number per pattern. Then, with $r = \alpha^2/\sigma^2$ and $\mathbf c = \mathbf V^\top\mathbf G^\top\mathbf d$, $\ln p(\mathbf d\mid\sigma^2,\alpha^2) = -\tfrac12\big[N_d\ln 2\pi\sigma^2 + \sum_i\ln(1 + r\mu_i) + \mathbf d^\top\mathbf d/\sigma^2 - (\alpha^2/\sigma^4)\sum_i c_i^2/(1 + r\mu_i)\big]$, and the conditional posterior has mean $r\,\mathbf V[\mathbf c/(1 + r\boldsymbol\mu)]$ and covariance $\alpha^2\mathbf V\,\mathrm{diag}(1/(1 + r\mu_i))\mathbf V^\top$. Every quantity below is evaluated on a whole grid of $(\sigma^2, \alpha^2)$ at once. The hyperprior here is log-uniform (uniform in $\ln\sigma^2$ and $\ln\alpha^2$ over the grid box); section 6 changes it.

def simdiag(G, DDm):
    mu, V = eigh(G.T @ G, DDm)
    return np.clip(mu, 0.0, None), V              # round-off can leave tiny negative eigenvalues where G is blind


def make_grid(ls2, la2):
    return np.meshgrid(np.exp(ls2), np.exp(la2), indexing="ij")


def log_marglik(d, G, mu, V, S2, A2):
    c = V.T @ G.T @ d
    q = 1.0 + (A2 / S2)[..., None] * mu
    ll = -0.5 * (d.size * np.log(2 * np.pi * S2) + np.log(q).sum(-1) + d @ d / S2 - (A2 / S2 ** 2) * (c ** 2 / q).sum(-1))
    return ll, c


def cond_moments(mu, V, c, s2, a2):
    """Conditional posterior means and marginal variances for arrays of (s2, a2)."""
    s2, a2 = np.atleast_1d(s2), np.atleast_1d(a2)
    r = (a2 / s2)[:, None]
    q = 1.0 + r * mu
    means = (r * (c / q)) @ V.T
    var = a2[:, None] * (1.0 / q) @ (V.T ** 2)
    return means, var


def analyse(d, G, mu, V, S2, A2, log_prior=0.0, s_true=None, wfloor=1e-7):
    ll, c = log_marglik(d, G, mu, V, S2, A2)
    i, j = np.unravel_index(np.argmax(ll), ll.shape)                      # ABIC = maximum marginal likelihood
    mp, vp = cond_moments(mu, V, c, S2[i, j], A2[i, j])
    lw = ll + log_prior
    w = np.exp(lw - lw.max()); w /= w.sum()
    keep = w > wfloor * w.max()
    ws = w[keep] / w[keep].sum()
    means, var = cond_moments(mu, V, c, S2[keep], A2[keep])
    mmix = ws @ means
    vmix = ws @ (var + means ** 2) - mmix ** 2
    out = dict(ll=ll, w=w, ij=(i, j), mp=mp[0], vp=vp[0], ws=ws, means=means, var=var, mmix=mmix, vmix=vmix,
               n_resolved=int(np.sum(A2[i, j] * mu / S2[i, j] > 1.0)))
    if s_true is not None:
        Fp = norm.cdf((s_true - out["mp"]) / np.sqrt(out["vp"]))
        Fm = (ws[:, None] * norm.cdf((s_true - means) / np.sqrt(var))).sum(0)
        out["cover_plug"] = float(np.mean((Fp > 0.05) & (Fp < 0.95)))
        out["cover_full"] = float(np.mean((Fm > 0.05) & (Fm < 0.95)))
    return out


def mixture_quantiles(ws, means, var, qs=(0.05, 0.95), n=600):
    """Quantiles of a Gaussian mixture, patch by patch, by evaluating its CDF on a fine grid."""
    lo = (means - 6 * np.sqrt(var)).min(0); hi = (means + 6 * np.sqrt(var)).max(0)
    out = np.empty((len(qs), means.shape[1]))
    for j in range(means.shape[1]):
        g = np.linspace(lo[j], hi[j], n)
        F = (ws[:, None] * norm.cdf((g[None, :] - means[:, j:j + 1]) / np.sqrt(var[:, j:j + 1]))).sum(0)
        out[:, j] = np.interp(qs, F, g)
    return out


ls2 = np.linspace(np.log(1e-4), np.log(400.0), 121)
la2 = np.linspace(np.log(a2_true) - 7, np.log(a2_true) + 7, 111)
S2, A2 = make_grid(ls2, la2)
Lc_prior = np.linalg.cholesky(a2_true * np.linalg.inv(DD))
cases = {"8 stations": np.geomspace(1, 40, 8), "40 stations": np.geomspace(0.5, 60, 40)}
ops = {name: (screw_G(xs, ze),) + simdiag(screw_G(xs, ze), DD) for name, xs in cases.items()}


def realization(k):
    """True slip drawn from the smoothing prior, and 40 noise values (the 8-station set uses the first 8)."""
    return Lc_prior @ np.random.default_rng(100 + k).standard_normal(M), sig_true * np.random.default_rng(200 + k).standard_normal(40)


cov30 = np.zeros((30, 4))                        # 30 realizations; the one drawn below is the most typical of them
for k in range(30):
    st, e = realization(k)
    for c_, (G, mu, V) in enumerate(ops.values()):
        o = analyse(G @ st + e[:G.shape[0]], G, mu, V, S2, A2, s_true=st)
        cov30[k, 2 * c_:2 * c_ + 2] = o["cover_plug"], o["cover_full"]
k_show = int(np.argmin(np.abs(cov30 - cov30.mean(0)).sum(1)))
print("share of patches inside the 90 %% intervals, mean of 30 realizations: 8 stations plug-in %.2f, fully Bayesian %.2f;"
      " 40 stations plug-in %.2f, fully Bayesian %.2f" % tuple(cov30.mean(0)))
print("realization drawn below: the one closest to these means (number %d: %.2f, %.2f; %.2f, %.2f)" % ((k_show,) + tuple(cov30[k_show])))
s_true2, e2 = realization(k_show)
sgn = np.sign(s_true2.sum())         # the prior is symmetric: a draw and its negative are equally typical, and flipping
s_true2, e2 = sgn * s_true2, sgn * e2   # slip and noise together leaves every coverage number unchanged; draw positive slip
single = {}
for name, (G, mu, V) in ops.items():
    o = analyse(G @ s_true2 + e2[:G.shape[0]], G, mu, V, S2, A2, s_true=s_true2)
    single[name] = (G, mu, V, o); i, j = o["ij"]
    print(f"{name}: noise rms {np.sqrt(np.mean(e2[:G.shape[0]] ** 2)):.2f} mm; ABIC choice sigma = {np.sqrt(S2[i, j]):.2f} mm,"
          f" alpha^2 = {A2[i, j]:.3g}; resolved combinations {o['n_resolved']};"
          f" mean slip sd: plug-in {np.sqrt(o['vp']).mean():.3f} m, fully Bayesian {np.sqrt(o['vmix']).mean():.3f} m")

    ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right")
fig.tight_layout()

How to read it. The realization drawn is the most typical of 30 (printed above), not a lucky or an unlucky one. Left: the grey regions are the posterior of the two knobs (the marginal likelihood times the log-uniform hyperprior); the cross is ABIC's single choice; the star marks the values used to generate the data. With 8 stations the posterior is broad, so ABIC's point is only one of many settings that explain the data about as well; with 40 stations it is compact and surrounds the values used to make the data. Right: the blue band is the 90 % interval of the plug-in posterior, the violet lines the 90 % interval of the fully Bayesian posterior. The fully Bayesian band is wider below the top few kilometres, where the data see the slip poorly and the knobs matter most. Even the compact 40-station posterior still spans a range of α² that widens the slip intervals at depth, and the badges show the plug-in bands missing the true slip more often.

One realization proves nothing about calibration. The next cell repeats the experiment many times, each time drawing a new true slip from the smoothing prior and new noise, and counts how often the 90 % intervals contain the true slip (the coverage; reminder: 2.01). The benchmark is 90 %: the posterior with the true knobs plugged in would reach it on average, because the true slips are drawn from that same prior.

In [5]:
def coverage_study(G, DDm, a2t, sigt, S2g, A2g, R, seed):
    rng_ = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    Mm = DDm.shape[0]
    mu_, V_ = simdiag(G, DDm)
    Lc_ = np.linalg.cholesky(a2t * np.linalg.inv(DDm) + 1e-12 * np.eye(Mm))
    cp, cf, ratio, nres, wid, wid_s, edge = [], [], [], [], [], [], []
    la_, ls_ = np.log(A2g[0]), np.log(S2g[:, 0])
    for _ in range(R):
        st = Lc_ @ rng_.standard_normal(Mm)
        dd_ = G @ st + sigt * rng_.standard_normal(G.shape[0])
        o_ = analyse(dd_, G, mu_, V_, S2g, A2g, s_true=st, wfloor=1e-6)
        cp.append(o_["cover_plug"]); cf.append(o_["cover_full"]); nres.append(o_["n_resolved"])
        ratio.append(np.mean(np.sqrt(o_["vmix"] / o_["vp"])))
        for w_, x_, out_ in [(o_["w"].sum(0), la_, wid), (o_["w"].sum(1), ls_, wid_s)]:   # spread of ln alpha^2 and ln sigma^2
            out_.append(np.sqrt((w_ * (x_ - (w_ * x_).sum()) ** 2).sum()))
        edge.append(o_["ij"][1] == 0)                 # ABIC optimum at the smallest alpha^2 of the grid: zero slip
    return dict(plug=np.mean(cp), full=np.mean(cf), ratio=np.mean(ratio), resolved=np.median(nres), sd_log_a2=np.median(wid),
                sd_log_s2=np.median(wid_s), edge=np.mean(edge))

How to read it. Each linked pair of markers is one data set-up repeated many times (table above): the plug-in in blue, the fully Bayesian answer in violet. The horizontal axis is how broad the posterior of the smoothing knob is. Where it is narrow, the two kinds of interval coincide and both contain the truth about 90 % of the time. As it broadens, the plug-in intervals miss the truth more and more often, and the fully Bayesian intervals become wider than the plug-in ones by the factor in the right panel. This is Fukuda & Johnson's dominant-peak condition, measured.

What makes the knob posterior broad? The small numbers in the right panel count the slip combinations that the data measure better than the prior does (generalised eigenvalues with $\alpha^2\mu_i/\sigma^2 > 1$): the fewer, the broader. Stations alone do not decide it: with the same 120 stations the antiplane fault resolves fewer combinations than the along-strike profile with its two sharpest kernels (table), because only the shallow part of the fault is seen. The two toys do not fall on one curve: the antiplane cases with 5 and 8 stations sit below the along-strike points of similar spread, and the table shows that their σ² posterior is also much broader (column sd ln s2). Our reading, an inference from this table, is that the uncertainty of σ² adds to that of α².

Two warnings for the weakest set-ups. The fully Bayesian intervals fall short of 90 % there too, because with data this weak the answer depends on the hyperprior, and even on where its range stops (section 6). And ABIC's optimum is, in a share of the repeats (last column), the smallest α² on the grid: nearly zero slip with nearly zero uncertainty.

Worked example (why the fully Bayesian interval is wider). For one patch the fully Bayesian variance obeys the law of total variance: $\mathrm{Var}[s_j\mid\mathbf d] = \mathrm{E}\big[\mathrm{Var}[s_j\mid\mathbf d,\sigma^2,\alpha^2]\big] + \mathrm{Var}\big[\mathrm{E}[s_j\mid\mathbf d,\sigma^2,\alpha^2]\big]$: the average spread for fixed knobs, plus how much the best estimate moves when the knobs move. The plug-in keeps only the first term, evaluated at one setting.

patch at 14.5 km depth, 8 stations:
  average conditional variance  E[Var]  = 0.02123 m^2
  variance of conditional means Var[E]  = 0.00072 m^2
  fully Bayesian variance (sum)         = 0.02196 m^2  (direct: 0.02196)

In this example the first term alone already exceeds the plug-in variance: the knob settings the data allow include larger σ² and α² than the ABIC pair, and those give a larger conditional spread. The second term adds less.

Common misreadings.

  • "ABIC is wrong." Without positivity it is the peak of the same posterior of the knobs (with a flat hyperprior), and Fukuda & Johnson (2010, p. 1449) give the condition under which the two answers agree. What the plug-in discards is the uncertainty of the knobs.
  • "Many stations make the knobs well determined." What counts is the number of independently resolved slip combinations and, for σ², the number of data left over after them.

In practice. A slip inversion that samples the smoothing scale and the data scales (with NUTS or another sampler) is the fully Bayesian column of this comparison. A plug-in answer understates the slip uncertainty most where the data resolve least.

3. Positivity breaks the ABIC formula¶

In plain words. Many slip inversions forbid slip in the wrong direction (back-slip on a thrust, for example). The closed-form ABIC formula averages over all slip models, including the forbidden negative ones. With positivity, the average must run over the allowed models only, and the share of the posterior that lies on the allowed side changes with the knobs. Leave that share out and ABIC picks the wrong knobs.

Precisely. Fukuda & Johnson (2008) state it in the abstract: "A popular objective method based on Akaike's Bayesian information criterion (ABIC) is incorrect if positivity constraints are employed" (p. 1128). In their appendix, the conventional procedure takes the non-negative least-squares (NNLS: least squares with every slip forced to be ≥ 0) solution $\mathbf s^\ast$ for each knob setting and evaluates the closed-form marginal likelihood (their eq. A7) with it, but "the analytical expression for the marginal likelihood, (A7), is derived from the prior PDF (9) that does not include positivity constraints" (p. 1146), and the correct integral "cannot be computed analytically" (p. 1145).

It can be computed numerically for a few patches. The positivity prior is the Gaussian prior truncated to $\mathbf s\ge 0$ (cut off below zero; reminder: truncated distributions, 2.11) and renormalised by $P(\mathbf s\ge\mathbf 0\mid\alpha^2)$ so that it integrates to one again. Integrating over the allowed region only gives

$$p_+(\mathbf d\mid\sigma^2,\alpha^2) = p(\mathbf d\mid\sigma^2,\alpha^2)\;\frac{P(\mathbf s\ge\mathbf 0\mid\mathbf d,\sigma^2,\alpha^2)}{P(\mathbf s\ge\mathbf 0\mid\alpha^2)},$$

where both probabilities are orthant probabilities of Gaussians: of the unconstrained posterior in the numerator, of the prior in the denominator. An orthant is the region where every coordinate has a fixed sign, here all positive: in two dimensions the positive quarter-plane, in three the positive eighth of space. An orthant probability is the share of a Gaussian's probability that falls inside it (in two dimensions, the share of the ellipse's probability in the quarter-plane). In closed form only for very few dimensions; here it is computed numerically for 8 patches. For a zero-mean prior the denominator does not depend on α², because scaling a zero-mean Gaussian leaves the share of it in the positive orthant unchanged. So the whole correction comes from the posterior, whose position relative to zero moves with the knobs. The picture below shows both statements in two dimensions.

In [8]:
# orthant probabilities in two dimensions: the share of a Gaussian in the quarter-plane where both slips are >= 0
rng_o = np.random.default_rng(31)
C_o = np.array([[1.0, 0.6], [0.6, 1.0]])                 # prior correlation of two neighbouring patches (m^2 per unit alpha^2)
G_o = np.array([[1.0, 0.4], [0.2, 0.7]])                 # two stations, two patches
d_o, s_o = np.array([0.35, 0.05]), 0.15                  # data and noise sd (same units as slip, for simplicity)


def post_o(a2):
    C = np.linalg.inv(np.linalg.inv(a2 * C_o) + G_o.T @ G_o / s_o ** 2)
    return C @ G_o.T @ d_o / s_o ** 2, C


def orthant_mc(m, C, n=2_000_000):
    return float(np.mean(np.all(rng_o.multivariate_normal(m, C, n) >= 0, axis=1)))


def ellipse90(m, C):
    ev, U = np.linalg.eigh(C)
    t_ = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200)
    return (m[:, None] + U @ (np.sqrt(ev * chi2_90)[:, None] * np.vstack([np.cos(t_), np.sin(t_)])))


chi2_90 = -2 * np.log(0.1)                                 # 90 % region of a 2-D Gaussian: Mahalanobis distance^2 < 4.61
rho_o = C_o[0, 1]
print(f"prior orthant probability, closed form 1/4 + arcsin(rho)/(2 pi) = {0.25 + np.arcsin(rho_o) / (2 * np.pi):.4f}")
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.7))
for ax, lim in zip(axs, [(-3.6, 3.6), (-0.55, 0.85)]):
    ax.fill_between([0, lim[1]], 0, lim[1], color="#ecebe6", lw=0, zorder=0)
    ax.axhline(0, color=S.AXIS, lw=0.8); ax.axvline(0, color=S.AXIS, lw=0.8)
    ax.set_xlim(*lim); ax.set_ylim(*lim); ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xlabel("slip of patch 1"); ax.set_ylabel("slip of patch 2")
    ax.text(lim[1] * 0.96, lim[1] * 0.93, "positive orthant\n(both slips ≥ 0)", ha="right", va="top", fontsize=8, color=S.INK2)
for a2, col in [(0.25, S.BLUE), (2.0, S.ORANGE)]:
    po = orthant_mc(np.zeros(2), a2 * C_o)
    e = ellipse90(np.zeros(2), a2 * C_o)
    axs[0].plot(e[0], e[1], color=col, lw=1.8, label=f"prior, α² = {a2:g}: P(both ≥ 0) = {po:.3f}")
    m_, C_ = post_o(a2)
    pp = orthant_mc(m_, C_)
    e = ellipse90(m_, C_)
    axs[1].plot(e[0], e[1], color=col, lw=1.8, label=f"posterior, α² = {a2:g}: P(both ≥ 0 | d) = {pp:.3f}")
    axs[1].plot(*m_, "o", color=col, ms=5)
    print(f"alpha^2 = {a2:4.2f}: prior orthant probability {po:.4f} (Monte Carlo), posterior {pp:.4f}, posterior mean {np.round(m_, 3)}")
axs[0].set_title("(a) Prior: the share does not depend on α²")
axs[1].set_title("(b) Posterior: the share moves with the knobs")
axs[1].plot([], [], "o", color=S.MUTED, ms=5, label="dots: posterior means")
for ax in axs:                                               # below the axes: the ellipses fill the panels

              title="curves: 90 % regions of the Gaussian (before the bound)", title_fontsize=7.4)

How to read it. Each curve is the 90 % region of a two-patch Gaussian; the shaded quarter-plane is the positive orthant. (a) Two zero-mean priors of different width: the larger one is the smaller one magnified about the origin, so the share of probability inside the quarter-plane is the same (printed, with the two-dimensional closed form). This is why the denominator of the formula above does not depend on α². (b) The posteriors for the same data at the same two settings sit at different places relative to the axes, so their shares differ (printed). That share is the numerator: it is what the conventional formula leaves out, and it changes with the knobs.

Test problem: 8 patches from 0 to 16 km, slip $(1.2, 1.5, 1.0, 0.3, 0, 0, 0, 0)$ m from the top down, 12 stations on one side, σ = 3 mm. The noise realization is chosen with a root-mean-square close to σ, so the example is typical (printed). Hyperpriors uniform in σ² and α², as in Fukuda & Johnson: "we assume that p(σ², α²) is a uniform PDF" (2008, p. 1131).

In [9]:
Mp = 8
zp = np.linspace(0.0, 16.0, Mp + 1)
xs_p = np.array([0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4.5, 6, 8, 11, 15, 20, 30, 45.0])
Np = xs_p.size
Gp = screw_G(xs_p, zp)
s_true_p = np.array([1.2, 1.5, 1.0, 0.3, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0])
e_p = 3.0 * np.random.default_rng(4).standard_normal(Np)
d_p = Gp @ s_true_p + e_p
print("noise realization rms: %.2f mm (sigma = 3 mm)" % np.sqrt(np.mean(e_p ** 2)))
Lp = second_difference(Mp)
LtLp = Lp.T @ Lp
P0p = np.linalg.inv(LtLp)
logdet_LtLp = np.linalg.slogdet(LtLp)[1]


def A_p(s2, a2):
    return Gp.T @ Gp / s2 + LtLp / a2


def f_p(s, s2, a2, d):
    r = d - Gp @ s
    q = Lp @ s
    return r @ r / s2 + q @ q / a2


def logml_A7(s, s2, a2, d):
    """Fukuda & Johnson (2008) eq. A7 with s plugged in: exact only when s is the unconstrained least-squares solution."""
    return (-0.5 * Np * np.log(2 * np.pi * s2) - 0.5 * Mp * np.log(a2) + 0.5 * logdet_LtLp
            - 0.5 * np.linalg.slogdet(A_p(s2, a2))[1] - 0.5 * f_p(s, s2, a2, d))


def s_free(s2, a2, d):
    return np.linalg.solve(A_p(s2, a2), Gp.T @ d / s2)


def s_nnls(s2, a2, d):
    return nnls(np.vstack([Gp / np.sqrt(s2), Lp / np.sqrt(a2)]), np.r_[d / np.sqrt(s2), np.zeros(Mp)])[0]


def log_orthant(m, C):
    return float(np.log(max(mvn(-m, C, allow_singular=True, seed=0).cdf(np.zeros(len(m))), 1e-300)))


def logml_exact(s2, a2, d, lp0):
    sf = s_free(s2, a2, d)
    C = np.linalg.inv(A_p(s2, a2)); C = 0.5 * (C + C.T)
    return logml_A7(sf, s2, a2, d) + log_orthant(sf, C) - lp0


for a2 in [0.01, 1.0, 100.0]:
    print("prior probability P(s >= 0 | alpha^2 = %6g) = %.5f" % (a2, np.exp(log_orthant(np.zeros(Mp), a2 * P0p))))
lp0 = log_orthant(np.zeros(Mp), P0p)

for i_, a in enumerate(ls2p):

        s2, a2 = np.exp(a), np.exp(b)
        sfree = s_free(s2, a2, d_p)
        free[i_, j_] = logml_A7(sfree, s2, a2, d_p)
        conv[i_, j_] = logml_A7(s_nnls(s2, a2, d_p), s2, a2, d_p)
        C_ = np.linalg.inv(A_p(s2, a2)); C_ = 0.5 * (C_ + C_.T)
        exact[i_, j_] = free[i_, j_] + log_orthant(sfree, C_) - lp0


def knob_posterior(F):
    W = F + ls2p[:, None] + la2p[None, :]           # uniform priors in sigma^2 and alpha^2 on a log grid: Jacobian
    W = np.exp(W - W.max()); W /= W.sum()
    return W


def grid_quantiles(p, x, qs=(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)):
    """Quantiles of a distribution given as probabilities p at grid points x (each point holds its whole cell)."""
    return np.interp(qs, np.cumsum(p) - 0.5 * p, x)


def gibbs_positive(d, n=20000, burn=2000, seed=1):
    """Exact Gibbs sampler of Fukuda & Johnson's model: truncated-normal slip, inverse-gamma sigma^2 and alpha^2."""
    r_ = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    s = np.maximum(np.linalg.lstsq(Gp, d, rcond=None)[0], 0.05); s2, a2 = 9.0, 1.0
    out = np.empty((n, Mp + 2))
    for it in range(n + burn):
        Ci = A_p(s2, a2); b = Gp.T @ d / s2
        for k in range(Mp):
            prec = Ci[k, k]; m_k = (b[k] - Ci[k] @ s + Ci[k, k] * s[k]) / prec; sd_k = 1.0 / np.sqrt(prec)
            s[k] = truncnorm.rvs(-m_k / sd_k, np.inf, loc=m_k, scale=sd_k, random_state=r_)
        res = d - Gp @ s
        s2 = (res @ res / 2) / r_.gamma(Np / 2 - 1)       # uniform prior on sigma^2 -> inverse gamma (N/2 - 1)
        q = Lp @ s
        a2 = (q @ q / 2) / r_.gamma(Mp / 2 - 1)           # uniform prior on alpha^2 -> inverse gamma (M/2 - 1)
        if it >= burn:
            out[it - burn] = np.r_[s, s2, a2]
    return out

The last lines check the computation itself. A Gibbs sampler is an MCMC method (reminder: Markov chains, 2.16) that updates one unknown at a time by drawing it from its exact conditional distribution given all the others; with positivity each conditional is a one-dimensional truncated Gaussian, easy to draw. The Monte Carlo error of the Gibbs sampler (2.05) and the grid step bound how closely the two exact methods can agree, and the grid must contain the posterior. Now the same comparison over 40 noise realizations, with σ held at its true value so that only the choice of α² differs.

How to read it. Left: the posterior of the smoothing knob under four computations. The exact positivity marginal likelihood (violet) and the exact Gibbs sampler of the full model (grey bars) agree, which validates the orthant formula; the conventional procedure (orange) and the formula without positivity (dashed blue) sit at larger α², that is, less smoothing (all numbers printed above). Middle: the conventional answer is a single NNLS solution whose error bars come from the unconstrained Gaussian covariance (their eq. A9), so they extend into negative slip that the model forbids. The fully Bayesian intervals respect positivity and are asymmetric near zero; the conventional intervals are also wider on average (printed). Right: over 40 noise realizations the conventional procedure chooses less smoothing than the exact answer every time (ratios printed above), the same direction as Fukuda & Johnson's Chi-Chi application, where the ABIC slip was "significantly rougher" than the fully Bayesian one and its uncertainty "significantly larger" (2008, p. 1137). The size of the effect here is specific to this small toy. The true slip is a sharp step that a smoothing prior does not expect, so neither answer recovers it exactly at the step; this comparison is about the choice of α² and the treatment of the bound, not about which interval covers better.

Common misreadings.

  • "With positivity the prior's normalising constant depends on α²." Not for a zero-mean prior: the prior orthant probability printed above is the same for all three α². The correction lives entirely in the posterior.
  • "A patch with zero true slip should have a posterior mean of zero." Under positivity the mean of a patch that the data cannot see is pulled above zero (the crosses), because the allowed values are all positive. Report intervals or medians.
  • "Impossible" in Fukuda & Johnson (2008) means not in closed form. The orthant probabilities are computable for a few patches (as here); for hundreds of patches they are not practical, which is why sampling is the general answer.

In practice. An ABIC slip model computed with positivity (non-negative least squares inside the ABIC loop) uses the formula this section shows to be wrong, so its smoothing weight and its error bars need that caveat. In a sampler the bound is simply part of the model and needs no special formula: notebook 2.33 (section 6) samples a positive slip model with NUTS.

4. Data weighting: several data sets with unknown noise levels¶

In plain words. Combining GPS and InSAR raises the same question: how much should each data set count? If both get the same weight, the 300 InSAR points outweigh the 25 more precise GPS points. In the hierarchical model each data set gets its own noise scale σ_k, and the data estimate them along with everything else.

Precisely. Fukuda & Johnson (2010) treat "multiple data sets with unknown relative weights, model parameters that are related linearly or non-linearly through theoretic models to observations" (p. 1441). With slip rates $\dot s_k$ entering linearly and locking depths $D_k$ nonlinearly, the slip rates can be integrated out in closed form for every $(D_1, D_2, \sigma_1, \sigma_2)$, so only four parameters need sampling: the mixed linear–nonlinear method. Their synthetic test has "25 observations with the smaller errors (data set 1) and 300 observations with the larger errors (data set 2). These two data sets might represent GPS and InSAR data, for example" (p. 1450), with noise sd 1.5 and 4.5 mm/yr. The geometry and true values below are chosen here (faults at −50 and 0 km, $\dot s = 25$ and 15 mm/yr, $D = 15$ and 10 km), not copied from the paper. Priors: $D_k$ uniform on 0.5–40 km, $\dot s_k \sim N(0, 50^2)$ mm/yr, $\ln\sigma_k$ uniform on (−3, 4).

In [14]:
x1f, x2f = -50.0, 0.0
truth4 = dict(s1=25.0, s2=15.0, D1=15.0, D2=10.0, sig1=1.5, sig2=4.5)
rng_pos = np.random.default_rng(5)
xg = np.sort(rng_pos.uniform(-250, 250, 25))
xi = np.sort(rng_pos.uniform(-150, 150, 300))
TAU = 50.0
Xall = jnp.asarray(np.r_[xg, xi])
grp = jnp.asarray(np.r_[np.zeros(25), np.ones(300)])
ramp = 0.02 * xi + 1.0                                         # used in section 5: an InSAR offset and orbital ramp (mm/yr)


def vel(x, s1, s2, D1, D2):
    return s1 / np.pi * np.arctan((x - x1f) / D1) + s2 / np.pi * np.arctan((x - x2f) / D2)


def make_data(seed, with_ramp=False):
    r_ = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    dg_ = vel(xg, truth4["s1"], truth4["s2"], truth4["D1"], truth4["D2"]) + truth4["sig1"] * r_.standard_normal(25)
    di_ = vel(xi, truth4["s1"], truth4["s2"], truth4["D1"], truth4["D2"]) + truth4["sig2"] * r_.standard_normal(300)
    if with_ramp:
        di_ = di_ + ramp
    return np.r_[dg_, di_]


def G_lin(D1, D2, with_ramp=False):
    cols = [jnp.arctan((Xall - x1f) / D1) / jnp.pi, jnp.arctan((Xall - x2f) / D2) / jnp.pi]
    if with_ramp:
        cols += [grp, grp * Xall / 100.0]                      # InSAR offset and ramp per 100 km, linear nuisances
    return jnp.stack(cols, 1)


def log_marg_lin(D1, D2, sig1, sig2, d, with_ramp=False):
    """ln p(d | D, sigma) with the linear parameters (slip rates, ramp) integrated out analytically."""
    G = G_lin(D1, D2, with_ramp)
    cinv = jnp.where(grp == 0, 1.0 / sig1 ** 2, 1.0 / sig2 ** 2)
    A = G.T @ (G * cinv[:, None]) + jnp.eye(G.shape[1]) / TAU ** 2
    b = G.T @ (cinv * d)
    c = jnp.linalg.cholesky(A)
    y = jax.scipy.linalg.solve_triangular(c, b, lower=True)
    return -0.5 * (d.size * jnp.log(2 * jnp.pi) - jnp.sum(jnp.log(cinv)) + 2 * jnp.sum(jnp.log(jnp.diag(c)))
                   + G.shape[1] * jnp.log(TAU ** 2) + jnp.sum(cinv * d ** 2) - y @ y)


def model_mixed(d, with_ramp=False, weights="separate", fixed_sig=3.0):
    D1 = numpyro.sample("D1", dist.Uniform(0.5, 40.0))
    D2 = numpyro.sample("D2", dist.Uniform(0.5, 40.0))
    if weights == "fixed":
        sig1 = sig2 = fixed_sig
    else:
        ls1 = numpyro.sample("log_sig1", dist.Uniform(-3.0, 4.0))
        ls2 = ls1 if weights == "common" else numpyro.sample("log_sig2", dist.Uniform(-3.0, 4.0))
        sig1, sig2 = jnp.exp(ls1), jnp.exp(ls2)
    numpyro.factor("marginal", log_marg_lin(D1, D2, sig1, sig2, d, with_ramp))


def model_joint(d):
    D1 = numpyro.sample("D1", dist.Uniform(0.5, 40.0)); D2 = numpyro.sample("D2", dist.Uniform(0.5, 40.0))
    s1 = numpyro.sample("s1", dist.Normal(0.0, TAU)); s2 = numpyro.sample("s2", dist.Normal(0.0, TAU))
    ls1 = numpyro.sample("log_sig1", dist.Uniform(-3.0, 4.0)); ls2 = numpyro.sample("log_sig2", dist.Uniform(-3.0, 4.0))
    mu_ = s1 * jnp.arctan((Xall - x1f) / D1) / jnp.pi + s2 * jnp.arctan((Xall - x2f) / D2) / jnp.pi
    numpyro.sample("obs", dist.Normal(mu_, jnp.where(grp == 0, jnp.exp(ls1), jnp.exp(ls2))), obs=d)


def run_nuts(model, seed=0, **kw):
    """4 NUTS chains. Returns the samples, the largest split R-hat and the number of divergent transitions."""
    mc = MCMC(NUTS(model), num_warmup=800, num_samples=1500, num_chains=4, chain_method="parallel", progress_bar=False)
    mc.run(jax.random.PRNGKey(seed), extra_fields=("diverging",), **kw)
    grouped = mc.get_samples(group_by_chain=True)
    rhat = max(float(np.max(split_gelman_rubin(np.asarray(v)))) for v in grouped.values())
    ndiv = int(np.sum(np.asarray(mc.get_extra_fields()["diverging"])))
    return {k: np.asarray(v) for k, v in mc.get_samples().items()}, rhat, ndiv


def sigmas_of(smp_, weights="separate", fixed_sig=3.0):
    n = smp_["D1"].size
    if weights == "fixed":
        return np.full(n, fixed_sig), np.full(n, fixed_sig)
    s1s = np.exp(smp_["log_sig1"])
    return s1s, (s1s if weights == "common" else np.exp(smp_["log_sig2"]))


def slip_rate_draws(smp_, d, weights="separate", fixed_sig=3.0, seed=0):
    """Draw the integrated-out slip rates from their Gaussian conditional, one draw per posterior sample."""
    r_ = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    s1s, s2s = sigmas_of(smp_, weights, fixed_sig)
    X = np.asarray(Xall); g = np.asarray(grp); dd_ = np.asarray(d)
    G = np.stack([np.arctan((X[None, :] - x1f) / smp_["D1"][:, None]),
                  np.arctan((X[None, :] - x2f) / smp_["D2"][:, None])], -1) / np.pi       # (samples, data, 2)
    cinv = np.where(g[None, :] == 0, 1 / s1s[:, None] ** 2, 1 / s2s[:, None] ** 2)
    A = np.einsum("kni,kn,knj->kij", G, cinv, G) + np.eye(2) / TAU ** 2
    b = np.einsum("kni,kn->ki", G, cinv * dd_[None, :])
    Ci = np.linalg.inv(A)
    return np.einsum("kij,kj->ki", Ci, b) + np.einsum("kij,kj->ki", np.linalg.cholesky(Ci), r_.standard_normal((len(s1s), 2)))


def q3(v):
    return np.percentile(v, [5, 50, 95])


t0 = time.time()
d4 = jnp.asarray(make_data(100))
sm, rh_m, dv_m = run_nuts(model_mixed, d=d4)
sj, rh_j, dv_j = run_nuts(model_joint, d=d4)
sc, rh_c, dv_c = run_nuts(model_mixed, d=d4, weights="common")
rates = slip_rate_draws(sm, d4)
print(f"{'parameter':10s} {'true':>6s} | {'mixed: 5 / 50 / 95 %':>24s} | {'full joint NUTS: 5 / 50 / 95 %':>30s}")
rows4 = [("D1 (km)", truth4["D1"], sm["D1"], sj["D1"]), ("D2 (km)", truth4["D2"], sm["D2"], sj["D2"]),
         ("s1 (mm/yr)", truth4["s1"], rates[:, 0], sj["s1"]), ("s2 (mm/yr)", truth4["s2"], rates[:, 1], sj["s2"]),
         ("sigma1", truth4["sig1"], np.exp(sm["log_sig1"]), np.exp(sj["log_sig1"])),
         ("sigma2", truth4["sig2"], np.exp(sm["log_sig2"]), np.exp(sj["log_sig2"]))]
for name, tv, a, b in rows4:
    qa, qb = q3(a), q3(b)
    print(f"{name:10s} {tv:6.2f} | {qa[0]:7.2f} {qa[1]:7.2f} {qa[2]:7.2f}  | {qb[0]:9.2f} {qb[1]:9.2f} {qb[2]:9.2f}")
print("one common sigma for both data sets: median %.2f mm/yr" % np.median(np.exp(sc["log_sig1"])))
for name, rh, dv in [("mixed", rh_m, dv_m), ("joint", rh_j, dv_j), ("common sigma", rh_c, dv_c)]:
    print(f"convergence, {name:12s}: largest split R-hat {rh:.3f}, divergent transitions {dv} (4 chains x 1500 draws)")
print("NUTS runs done in %.0f s" % (time.time() - t0))

Worked example (integrating the slip rates out by hand). For one setting of $(D_1, D_2, \sigma_1, \sigma_2)$ the closed form needs only a 2 × 2 matrix $\mathbf A = \mathbf G^\top\mathbf C_d^{-1}\mathbf G + \mathbf I/\tau^2$ and the vector $\mathbf b = \mathbf G^\top\mathbf C_d^{-1}\mathbf d$. The cell prints them and checks the closed form against a brute-force sum of $p(\mathbf d\mid\dot s_1,\dot s_2)\,p(\dot s_1,\dot s_2)$ over a fine grid of slip rates.

In [15]:
D1w, D2w, sg1w, sg2w = 15.0, 10.0, 1.5, 4.5
Gw = np.asarray(G_lin(D1w, D2w)); cinvw = np.where(np.asarray(grp) == 0, 1 / sg1w ** 2, 1 / sg2w ** 2); dw = np.asarray(d4)
Aw = Gw.T @ (Gw * cinvw[:, None]) + np.eye(2) / TAU ** 2; bw = Gw.T @ (cinvw * dw)
print("A =\n", np.round(Aw, 4)); print("b =", np.round(bw, 4))
print("conditional mean of the slip rates A^-1 b =", np.round(np.linalg.solve(Aw, bw), 3), "mm/yr")
cf_val = float(log_marg_lin(D1w, D2w, sg1w, sg2w, d4))
g1 = np.linspace(20, 32, 401); g2 = np.linspace(9, 23, 401); dg1, dg2 = g1[1] - g1[0], g2[1] - g2[0]
S1g, S2gr = np.meshgrid(g1, g2, indexing="ij")
pred = S1g[..., None] * Gw[:, 0] + S2gr[..., None] * Gw[:, 1]
loglik = -0.5 * np.sum(cinvw * (dw - pred) ** 2, -1) - 0.5 * dw.size * np.log(2 * np.pi) + 0.5 * np.sum(np.log(cinvw))
logprior = -0.5 * (S1g ** 2 + S2gr ** 2) / TAU ** 2 - np.log(2 * np.pi * TAU ** 2)
mx = (loglik + logprior).max()
brute = mx + np.log(np.sum(np.exp(loglik + logprior - mx)) * dg1 * dg2)
print(f"closed-form ln p(d | D, sigma) = {cf_val:.4f};  brute-force sum over slip rates = {brute:.4f}")

How to read it. The table above shows that integrating the slip rates out (mixed method, four sampled parameters) gives the same posterior as sampling all six parameters, and the worked example confirms the closed form against a brute-force sum. The estimated noise scales land near the values used to make the data. Forcing one common σ makes each GPS point count only as much as an InSAR point, so the locking depths spread more (right panel; widths printed).

One realization again; the next cell repeats the inversion for new noise and counts how often the 90 % intervals of the four physical parameters contain the true values, for three weighting choices: separate σ_k estimated, one common σ estimated, and both σ fixed by hand at 3 mm/yr (between the two true values).

With only 12 realizations each share scatters by the binomial error printed above, so only large departures mean something. Read the table in two steps. The hand-fixed weights give the narrowest intervals and miss the truth far more often than one time in ten: σ = 3 mm/yr over-trusts the 300 InSAR points (true scatter 4.5) and under-trusts the 25 GPS points (true scatter 1.5), and the intervals do not know it. The common σ is estimated, so its intervals are honest about the total misfit, but every GPS point now counts only as much as an InSAR point, and the intervals are wider than with separate σ_k. The separate σ_k let each data set count as much as its scatter justifies.

Common misreadings.

  • "Weighting by the number of points is the fix." The number of points is already in the likelihood; what is unknown is each set's noise level, and that is what σ_k estimates.
  • "The estimated σ_k is the instrument noise." Only if the model is right. Section 5.

In practice. Joint inversions of GNSS, InSAR and other data sets estimate exactly these σ_k. Fukuda & Johnson (2010) sampled the nonlinear parameters and the σ_k with a Metropolis random walk (2.16) and integrated the linear ones out, as here; with NUTS (2.18) the same closed-form marginal enters as one numpyro.factor term (code above), which simply adds that log marginal likelihood to the log density the sampler explores.

5. Estimated weights measure misfit, not instrument quality¶

In plain words. The data weight is estimated from how badly the model misses each data set. Any miss counts: noise, but also anything the model cannot represent. If the InSAR data contain an orbital ramp that the model lacks, the shared fault parameters bend to absorb part of it, then miss the GPS data, and the GPS weight drops.

Precisely. Add an offset and linear ramp, $1 + 0.02\,x$ mm/yr ($x$ in km), to the InSAR-like data only. Invert (a) without modelling it and (b) with offset and ramp as two extra linear parameters for the InSAR set (integrated out like the slip rates). Ten noise realizations.

In [18]:
t0 = time.time()
print("ramp over the InSAR points: rms %.2f mm/yr about its mean, %.2f mm/yr including its offset (InSAR noise sd 4.5)"
      % (np.sqrt(np.mean((ramp - ramp.mean()) ** 2)), np.sqrt(np.mean(ramp ** 2))))


def residual_rms(smp_, d, with_ramp):
    """GPS and InSAR residual rms at the posterior medians of D and sigma, linear parameters at their conditional mean."""
    s1m, s2m = np.exp(np.median(smp_["log_sig1"])), np.exp(np.median(smp_["log_sig2"]))
    G = np.asarray(G_lin(np.median(smp_["D1"]), np.median(smp_["D2"]), with_ramp)); g = np.asarray(grp); dd_ = np.asarray(d)
    cinv = np.where(g == 0, 1 / s1m ** 2, 1 / s2m ** 2)
    A = G.T @ (G * cinv[:, None]) + np.eye(G.shape[1]) / TAU ** 2
    r = dd_ - G @ np.linalg.solve(A, G.T @ (cinv * dd_))
    return np.sqrt(np.mean(r[g == 0] ** 2)), np.sqrt(np.mean(r[g == 1] ** 2))


res5, rms5, worst5 = [], [], [1.0, 0]
for rep in range(10):
    dd = jnp.asarray(make_data(200 + rep, with_ramp=True))
    row, rrow = [], []
    for wr in [False, True]:
        s_, rh_, dv_ = run_nuts(model_mixed, seed=rep, d=dd, with_ramp=wr)
        worst5 = [max(worst5[0], rh_), worst5[1] + dv_]
        row.append([np.median(np.exp(s_["log_sig1"])), np.median(np.exp(s_["log_sig2"])), np.median(s_["D1"]), np.median(s_["D2"])])
        rrow.append(residual_rms(s_, dd, wr))
    res5.append(row); rms5.append(rrow)
res5, rms5 = np.array(res5), np.array(rms5)
for k, lab in enumerate(["ramp ignored", "ramp modelled"]):
    med = np.median(res5[:, k], 0)
    print(f"{lab:14s}: median over 10 realizations of the posterior medians: sigma1 {med[0]:.2f}, sigma2 {med[1]:.2f} mm/yr,"
          f" D1 {med[2]:.1f} km, D2 {med[3]:.1f} km   (true 1.5, 4.5, 15, 10)")
    print(f"{'':14s}  residual rms (median over realizations): GPS {np.median(rms5[:, k, 0]):.2f}, InSAR {np.median(rms5[:, k, 1]):.2f} mm/yr")
print("InSAR residual rms if the whole ramp had stayed in the residuals: %.2f mm/yr"
      % np.sqrt(np.median(rms5[:, 1, 1]) ** 2 + np.mean(ramp ** 2)))
print("realizations where ignoring the ramp raised the GPS sigma1: %d of 10; deepened D1: %d of 10"
      % (np.sum(res5[:, 0, 0] > res5[:, 1, 0]), np.sum(res5[:, 0, 2] > res5[:, 1, 2])))
print("over all 20 runs: largest split R-hat %.3f, divergent transitions %d  (%.0f s)" % (worst5[0], worst5[1], time.time() - t0))

saved figures/2-30_weights_absorb_misfit.png

How to read it. Each line is one realization; the two noise scales are drawn as ratios to their true values on one axis. Ignoring the ramp (orange) raises the estimated GPS noise scale well above its true value and pushes the locking depth of fault 1 deeper, while the InSAR scale, whose data contain the ramp, hardly moves (medians printed above). Modelling the ramp (violet) brings all three back. The printed residuals show the mechanism. With the ramp ignored, the InSAR residual grows far less than it would if the ramp had stayed in the residuals, so the fault parameters have absorbed most of the ramp; the GPS residual grows, because the shifted fault parameters no longer fit the GPS points. The GPS weight is then lowered to accommodate a misfit that the GPS data did not cause.

So an estimated σ_k is "how far the model misses this data set", which equals the instrument noise only when the model can represent everything in the data. This is the rule notebook 2.13 found from the other side: a noise scale fitted to the residuals responds to how large the misfit is, not to how the model error affects the parameters. Two remedies: model the systematic part explicitly (here the ramp), or describe it with a correlated prediction-error covariance $\mathbf C_p$ (notebook 2.13; Duputel et al. 2014), which a single scale factor per data set cannot represent.

In practice. Many InSAR inversions estimate an offset and a planar ramp per interferogram as extra linear parameters, which is the first remedy shown here. Read the posterior σ_k as the misfit level of each data set given the model, not as data quality. A large σ_k for one data set can come from a model error that enters through another data set, and any relative weight formed from two σ_k inherits that.

6. The hyperprior is part of the model¶

In plain words. "Let the data decide" still needs a prior on the knobs, and "uniform" depends on the scale you call uniform. A prior that is flat in α² from 10⁻⁵ to 10⁵ puts most of its probability in the top decade (printed below), a strong preference for weak smoothing. A prior flat in ln α² treats every decade the same.

Precisely. Three hyperpriors on the data scale: uniform in σ² (Fukuda & Johnson 2008: "we assume that p(σ², α²) is a uniform PDF", p. 1131; 2010: "We thus assume that p(σ, α) is constant if all the components of σ and α are positive", p. 1446, where their σ is the vector of the σ_k²), log-uniform in σ (scale-invariant: the same probability for every decade, so the answer does not depend on the units), and HalfCauchy(1) on the factor σ/σ_nominal (the positive half of a Cauchy distribution, 2.03: centred at zero with a heavy tail that still allows large values; a common weakly informative choice, Gelman 2006; σ_nominal = 2 mm here). Two on the smoothing knob over [10⁻⁵, 10⁵]: uniform in α², as in Zhao & Jiang (2026): "We set a uniform prior of [10⁻⁵, 10⁵] for α²" (p. 5), and uniform in ln α². Test: the antiplane fault in depth with 8 and with 40 stations; one realization for the posteriors, then 200 realizations for coverage.

In [20]:
print("prior probability of alpha^2 > 1e4 under a uniform prior on [1e-5, 1e5]: %.3f" % ((1e5 - 1e4) / (1e5 - 1e-5)))
ls2_6 = np.linspace(np.log(0.01), np.log(400.0), 90)
la2_6 = np.linspace(np.log(1e-5), np.log(1e5), 161)
S2_6, A2_6 = make_grid(ls2_6, la2_6)
sig_nom = 2.0


def log_hyperprior(kind_s, kind_a):
    if kind_s == "uniform in σ²":
        lp_s = ls2_6[:, None] * 1.0
    elif kind_s == "log-uniform":
        lp_s = np.zeros((ls2_6.size, 1))
    else:                                                   # HalfCauchy(1) on k = sigma / sigma_nominal
        k = np.sqrt(np.exp(ls2_6)) / sig_nom
        lp_s = (np.log(k) - np.log1p(k ** 2))[:, None]
    lp_a = la2_6[None, :] * 1.0 if kind_a == "uniform in α²" else np.zeros((1, la2_6.size))
    return lp_s + lp_a


kinds_s = ["uniform in σ²", "log-uniform", "HalfCauchy(1) on σ/2 mm"]
kinds_a = ["uniform in α²", "uniform in ln α²"]
post6 = {}
for name, xs in cases.items():
    G = screw_G(xs, ze); mu, V = simdiag(G, DD)
    e6 = sig_true * np.random.default_rng(7).standard_normal(xs.size)
    d = G @ s_true2 + e6
    print(f"{name} (noise rms of this realization {np.sqrt(np.mean(e6 ** 2)):.2f} mm)")
    for ks in kinds_s:
        for ka in kinds_a:
            o = analyse(d, G, mu, V, S2_6, A2_6, log_prior=log_hyperprior(ks, ka), s_true=s_true2)
            pa, ps = o["w"].sum(0), o["w"].sum(1)
            qa = np.exp(grid_quantiles(pa, la2_6))
            qs = np.exp(0.5 * grid_quantiles(ps, ls2_6)[1])
            post6[name, ks, ka] = pa
            print(f"   σ prior {ks:24s} α² prior {ka:17s}: α² median {qa[1]:.3g} [90 %: {qa[0]:.2g}, {qa[2]:.2g}],"
                  f" σ median {qs:.2f} mm, mean slip sd {np.sqrt(o['vmix']).mean():.3f} m")

t0 = time.time()
cov6 = {}
for name, xs in cases.items():
    G = screw_G(xs, ze); mu, V = simdiag(G, DD); rng6 = np.random.default_rng(21)
    for ka in kinds_a:
        cv, sdv = [], []
        rng6 = np.random.default_rng(21)
        for rep in range(200):
            st = Lc_prior @ rng6.standard_normal(M); dd = G @ st + sig_true * rng6.standard_normal(xs.size)
            o = analyse(dd, G, mu, V, S2_6, A2_6, log_prior=log_hyperprior("log-uniform", ka), s_true=st, wfloor=1e-6)
            cv.append(o["cover_full"]); sdv.append(np.sqrt(o["vmix"]).mean())
        cov6[name, ka] = (np.mean(cv), np.mean(sdv))
        print(f"{name:12s} α² prior {ka:17s}: coverage of 90 % intervals {np.mean(cv):.3f}, mean slip sd {np.mean(sdv):.3f} m")
print("(%.0f s)" % (time.time() - t0))

Weak data: where does the prior stop? A log-uniform prior is improper at zero (it cannot be normalised; reminder: improper priors, 2.09 and 2.11): its integral over ln α² diverges as α² → 0, and only the end of the grid keeps it finite. That is harmless when the data rule out tiny α², but not when the data could be pure noise. The next cell takes the weakest set-up of section 2 (along-strike profile, 6 stations, 30 km kernel) and moves the lower end of the α² range down, for three hyperpriors: log-uniform; flat in α²; and a HalfCauchy prior on the scale α (not α²), which is proper at zero. Its scale is put at the value used to make the data, an oracle choice that no real inversion has, so scales ten times smaller and larger are printed too. The upper end stays where section 2 put it.

t0 = time.time()
xs_w = np.linspace(0.5, Ms - 0.5, 6)
K_w = np.exp(-0.5 * ((xs_w[:, None] - xa[None, :]) / 30.0) ** 2); K_w /= K_w.sum(1, keepdims=True)
mu_w, V_w = simdiag(K_w, DDs)
Lc_w = np.linalg.cholesky(a2s * np.linalg.inv(DDs) + 1e-12 * np.eye(Ms))
ls2_w = np.linspace(np.log(1e-4), np.log(10.0), 81)
lowers = [7, 10, 14]                                 # lower end of the alpha^2 range, in ln-units below the true value


def weak_coverage(lower, prior, scale=1.0, R=100, seed=300):
    la2_w = np.arange(np.log(a2s) - lower, np.log(a2s) + 7 + 1e-9, 14 / 110)
    S2w, A2w = make_grid(ls2_w, la2_w)
    if prior == "log-uniform":
        lp = 0.0
    elif prior == "flat in α²":
        lp = la2_w[None, :] * 1.0
    else:                                            # HalfCauchy on alpha, written as a density in ln alpha^2
        lp = (0.5 * la2_w - np.log1p(np.exp(la2_w) / (scale ** 2 * a2s)))[None, :]
    r_ = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    cf, cp, edge, low = [], [], [], []
    for _ in range(R):
        st = Lc_w @ r_.standard_normal(Ms)
        o_ = analyse(K_w @ st + 0.5 * r_.standard_normal(6), K_w, mu_w, V_w, S2w, A2w, log_prior=lp, s_true=st, wfloor=1e-6)
        cf.append(o_["cover_full"]); cp.append(o_["cover_plug"]); edge.append(o_["ij"][1] == 0)
        low.append(o_["w"].sum(0)[la2_w < np.log(a2s) - 4].sum())     # posterior share far below the true alpha^2
    return np.mean(cf), np.mean(cp), np.mean(edge), np.mean(low)


weak = {p: [weak_coverage(lo, p) for lo in lowers] for p in ["log-uniform", "flat in α²", "HalfCauchy on α"]}
for p, rows in weak.items():
    print(f"{p:16s}: coverage of the fully Bayesian 90 % intervals for lower ends " +
          ", ".join(f"-{lo}: {r[0]:.3f}" for lo, r in zip(lowers, rows)) +
          "; posterior share more than 4 ln-units below the true alpha^2: " + ", ".join(f"{r[3]:.2f}" for r in rows))
print("ABIC plug-in for the same lower ends: coverage " + ", ".join(f"{r[1]:.3f}" for r in weak["log-uniform"]) +
      "; share of realizations whose ABIC optimum is the lowest alpha^2: " + ", ".join(f"{r[2]:.2f}" for r in weak["log-uniform"]))
print("HalfCauchy on alpha with its scale 10 times smaller / larger (lower end -7): coverage %.3f / %.3f"
      % (weak_coverage(7, "HalfCauchy on α", 0.1)[0], weak_coverage(7, "HalfCauchy on α", 10.0)[0]))
G5 = screw_G(XS_AP[5], ze); mu5, V5 = simdiag(G5, DD)

    r_ = np.random.default_rng(5); meds = []

        meds.append(np.exp(0.5 * grid_quantiles(o_["w"].sum(1), np.log(S2s[:, 0]))[1]))
    print(f"antiplane fault, 5 stations, log-uniform prior on sigma^2 down to {lo_s2:g} mm^2: median of the posterior medians of sigma {np.median(meds):.2f} mm (true 2)")

How to read it. (a, b) The data-noise prior matters only when data are few (σ medians printed above). The smoothing-knob prior matters even with 40 stations: a prior flat in α² drags the posterior towards weaker smoothing and inflates the slip uncertainty (printed). The reason is that the data constrain α² only loosely (the 90 % ranges printed above span large factors), and across such a range a prior flat in α² has a density proportional to α² on the logarithmic axis, which tilts the posterior towards the upper end. (c) In this test, where the true slip is drawn from the smoothing prior, the log-uniform choice gives close to nominal coverage and the flat-in-α² choice over-covers. Over-coverage means intervals that are too wide, which is safer than too narrow but still a statement about the prior, not the data.

(d) With the weakest data the log-uniform coverage keeps falling as the lower end of its range moves down: the posterior piles up at tiny α² (the printed share far below the true value grows), that is, at nearly zero slip with a small uncertainty. ABIC fails in its own way here: in a share of the realizations (printed) its optimum is the lowest α² on offer, which means nearly zero slip with nearly zero uncertainty. The flat prior ignores the lower end but over-covers strongly. The HalfCauchy prior does not depend on the lower end, and at the oracle scale its coverage is close to 90 %, but it moves far from 90 % when the scale is ten times off (printed). With data this weak no hyperprior is neutral: the answer is mostly the prior. The same happens to σ² when there are fewer data than slip patches. The slip can then fit the data exactly, the likelihood stays finite as σ² → 0, and under a log-uniform prior the posterior of σ depends on where its range stops (printed for 5 stations).

Common misreadings.

  • "A uniform hyperprior is uninformative." Uniform in which variable? Over ten decades, uniform in α² is very informative about α².
  • "The hyperprior washes out with enough data." Only for knobs the data pin down. The smoothing knob of a slip model is informed by the handful of resolved slip combinations (section 2), so its prior keeps mattering.
  • "A grid or sampler range is a technical detail." For a prior that is improper at one end, the end of the range is the prior there, and with weak data it decides the answer (panel d).

In practice. Fukuda & Johnson (2008, 2010) use priors flat in σ² and α²; Zhao & Jiang (2026) use the prior flat in α² quoted above (notebook 2.31 examines their method). A log-normal prior on a scale is proper at both ends, so the range problem of panel (d) cannot arise, but its median and width are choices a swap test should check. In this test HalfCauchy(1) on σ/σ_nominal behaves like the log-uniform prior for σ (σ medians printed above). Gelman (2006) discusses the failure of log-uniform priors for hierarchical scale parameters and recommends half-Cauchy priors on the scale instead. Whichever is used, state it and check whether the answer moves when it is swapped, as done here.

7. What "objective" buys and what it does not¶

approach chosen by the analyst estimated from the data uncertainty of the knobs
hand-tuned / L-curve (2.29) λ (by eye), smoothing operator, noise model nothing ignored
ABIC (empirical Bayes) smoothing operator, noise model σ², α² as single best values ignored; wrong formula under positivity
fully Bayesian (hierarchical) smoothing operator, noise model, hyperpriors σ², α² as distributions propagated into the slip
+ data weights σ_k grouping of the data, independence of errors one scale per data set propagated, but σ_k absorb model error

The fully Bayesian approach is the most complete of these, but every row still rests on choices: the form of the smoothing prior (is slip really smooth?), the error model (independent Gaussian? correlated? model errors?), and the hyperpriors. How much those choices matter depends on the data. Where the data resolve many slip combinations, ABIC and the fully Bayesian answer agree (section 2). Where they resolve few, the plug-in is overconfident and the fully Bayesian answer leans on the hyperprior (section 6), until with the weakest data the answer is mostly the prior; objectivity is then something the data cannot provide. The next notebook asks the first of these questions directly: should slip be smoothed at all?

In practice.

  • Sampling the smoothing scale (often non-centered, $\mathbf m = \alpha\mathbf u$) with one sampled σ_k per data set is the fully Bayesian row with data weights. Notebook 2.33 adds a caution: with strong data the centered form of the scale can be the better-behaved one, so check divergences in both forms.
  • A prior whose length scale and smoothness are held fixed in a run (for example a Matérn prior) leaves their uncertainty out of the error bars. Choosing them from a grid of runs by the evidence is the ABIC row of the table; choosing them by eye is the hand-tuned row.
  • Read every estimated weight as a misfit level (section 5), and compare fits per data set by WRMS and χ² (2.29, section 7).
